title: Sea Level to Summit, Running Monaco's Hinterland

bestPeriod.note: July and August bring heat above 30°C and prefectural fire closures on the limestone massifs.

basecamps: Monaco (or Beausoleil, 200 m across the border)
summary: A Riviera running week from a two-square-kilometre basecamp, climbing straight from the Mediterranean to the 900 m limestone ridges above Monaco.
hook: Monaco is two square kilometres and you can run across it in eleven minutes. That is precisely why it works: the border is invisible, the mountains start at the last apartment block, and within twenty minutes of leaving the port you are on a limestone path with nothing but sea below you. Everything in this week except the first and last kilometre happens in France.

snapshot.Country: Monaco (routes run into the Alpes-Maritimes, France)
snapshot.Base(s): Monaco or Beausoleil, with runs from Cap d'Ail, La Turbie, Èze, Roquebrune and Menton
snapshot.Best Period: March to May and October to November
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 115-125 km and 5,800-6,400 m of ascent; limestone, pine needle, scree, stone stairway and coastal path, T1-T3
snapshot.Getting There: Fly Nice (NCE), then the airport express bus or tram plus TER to Monaco-Monte-Carlo (approx. 45-60 min)
snapshot.Who It Suits: Runners who like relentless gradient, sea views and a base where dinner costs more than the flight

itinerary.title: The Sentier du Littoral, Sea Level
itinerary.morning: Arrive, drop bags, and start with Monaco's own peculiar terrain: the public lifts and escalators linking the tiers of the city, and the stone ramps to the Rocher. The Rampe Major from port to Palace is the classic, a genuine strength session if you take it four times.
itinerary.afternoon: Train or run west to Cap d'Ail and pick up the Sentier du Littoral below the Cap, from Plage Marquet round to Plage Mala. Rock-cut steps, sea spray, pine tunnels and a few exposed sections above the water, T2 because of the steps, not the difficulty.
itinerary.evening: Eat in the Condamine market hall, which is the only sensible-value food in the Principality.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km, 400 m ascent, T1-T2. Water: public taps at Plage Marquet and Plage Mala (seasonal, spring to autumn), fountains throughout Monaco's parks. **Bail-out:** Cap-d'Ail station sits directly above the path.

itinerary.title: Mont des Mules and the Trophée
itinerary.morning: Climb out of Beausoleil on the Sentier du Mont des Mules, the botanical path up the 520 m limestone knuckle behind Monaco. Short, sharp, well-marked T2, with an Iron Age oppidum on top.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue north towards La Turbie and the Trophée des Alpes, Augustus's 6 BC victory monument on the Grande Corniche at 480 m, then drop back down the old mule path to Beausoleil.
itinerary.evening: Stretch. The gradient is unforgiving in both directions and the descents are what hurt.
itinerary.dayStats: 15 km, 750 m ascent, T2. Water: the village fountain in La Turbie's old centre, reliable year-round; nothing on the Mont des Mules loop. **Bail-out:** the Monaco-La Turbie bus runs from the village square down to Monaco.

itinerary.title: Tête de Chien and the Grande Corniche
itinerary.morning: Train one stop to Cap-d'Ail, then climb to the Tête de Chien, the 550 m headland hanging directly over Monaco, capped by a 19th-century fort that is military property and closed. The path to the belvedere edge is public, and the view down onto the Rocher is the defining image of the region.
itinerary.afternoon: Traverse north to La Turbie on the Grande Corniche paths, then descend the long ridge line back towards Monaco. Roughly 800 m of climbing with a fast, stony descent, T2, with short T3 steps where the path crosses slab.
itinerary.evening: Larvotto for a swim, around 16-18°C in April, 20-22°C in October.
itinerary.dayStats: 17 km, 830 m ascent, T2-T3. Water: La Turbie village fountain; the Golf de Monte-Carlo clubhouse at La Turbie serves non-members. **Bail-out:** drop west to Èze-sur-Mer or east to Cap-d'Ail, both on the Nice-Ventimiglia line.

itinerary.title: Cap Martin, Deliberately Flat
itinerary.morning: Recovery day. Train to Roquebrune-Cap-Martin and run the Promenade Le Corbusier round the headland to Menton, a paved and rock-cut sea-level path past the Cabanon Le Corbusier built for himself in 1952 and the villa Eileen Gray designed above it.
itinerary.afternoon: Menton: the Marché des Halles, the old-town stairways to the cemetery terrace, then the train home.
itinerary.evening: Early bed. Tomorrow is the big one.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km, 250 m ascent, T1. Water: fountains along the Carnolès promenade and in Menton's old town. **Bail-out:** three stations within 5 km of any point on this route.

itinerary.title: Peak Day: Sainte-Agnès, Col de la Madone, Mont Agel
itinerary.morning: First train to Menton, then climb the old path towards Sainte-Agnès, at 800 m the highest coastal village in Europe and a fortified balcony above the sea. It is a sustained 800 m of hot, stony, exposed T2 climbing, start at first light.
itinerary.afternoon: Contour west to the Col de la Madone at 925 m, the pass professional cyclists use for testing, then work along the flank of Mont Agel. Be clear about Agel: its 1,148 m summit is a French Air Force radar station, permanently closed. The runnable ground is the shoulder below it, past the Golf de Monte-Carlo course at around 900 m, then the long descent through La Turbie to Monaco.
itinerary.dayStats: 30 km, 1,750 m ascent, T2 with T3 sections above Sainte-Agnès. Water: Sainte-Agnès village fountain at 8 km, Gorbio village fountain on the alternative line, La Turbie at 24 km. Carry 2 l, the Madone traverse is dry and shadeless. **Bail-out:** descend from Sainte-Agnès or Gorbio to Menton, both served by local buses; from La Turbie, the bus to Monaco.

itinerary.title: Parc de la Grande Corniche and the Sentier Nietzsche
itinerary.morning: Bus or train west to Èze and into the Parc naturel départemental de la Grande Corniche. Run the plateau paths past the Fort de la Revère at 740 m, a Second Empire fort now a viewpoint and picnic area, over the Plateau de la Justice and the Mont Bataille top on the ridge above La Turbie.
itinerary.afternoon: Drop to Mont Bastide, the Ligurian hill settlement above Èze village, then descend the Sentier Nietzsche, the stepped path the philosopher walked while composing part of *Zarathustra*, 400 m to Èze-sur-Mer. Steep, stony, T2, hard on tired quads.
itinerary.evening: Train back along the coast at sunset.
itinerary.dayStats: 19 km, 900 m ascent, T2. Water: the picnic area at the Fort de la Revère has a tap that runs seasonally, do not plan on it; the fountains in Èze village are dependable. **Bail-out:** the Moyenne Corniche bus between Nice and Beausoleil stops at Èze village; Èze-sur-Mer station is at the bottom of the Sentier Nietzsche.

itinerary.title: Stairs, Gardens, Departure
itinerary.morning: Shakeout inside the Principality: the Jardin Exotique cliff terraces, the Parc Princesse Antoinette, then down through the public lifts to the port and a lap of Larvotto.
itinerary.afternoon: Coffee on the Place d'Armes, then the train or express bus to Nice airport.
itinerary.dayStats: 8 km, 300 m ascent, mostly stairs and paved terrace, T1.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel Olympia
accommodationStrategy.description: Two hundred metres over the French border and roughly a third of Monaco's room rate, which is the single biggest saving available on this trip. It also sits at the foot of the Mont des Mules path, so Day 2 starts at the door and every La Turbie run begins uphill from reception.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three months ahead; avoid Grand Prix weekend entirely.

accommodationStrategy.name: Novotel Monte-Carlo
accommodationStrategy.description: Built into the slope above the station on Boulevard Princesse Charlotte, with a pool, a garden terrace and direct lift access down to the port. Being on top of Monaco-Monte-Carlo station matters when four of the week's days start with a train.
accommodationStrategy.booking: four months ahead in spring and autumn.

logistics.emergency: works in both Monaco and France; inside the Principality 17 is police and 18 fire and medical. In the French hinterland rescue comes through 112, name the commune and the nearest marked path.

other.text: works in both Monaco and France; inside the Principality 17 is police and 18 fire and medical. In the French hinterland rescue comes through 112, name the commune and the nearest marked path.
There are no border controls and the currency is the euro, but EU roaming does not apply on Monaco's own network, lock your phone onto a French operator.

The TER Nice-Ventimiglia line is the backbone: every 20-30 minutes, stopping at Cap-d'Ail, Monaco-Monte-Carlo, Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, Carnolès and Menton. Buy on SNCF Connect; validate any paper ticket before boarding.
Zou! bus line 100 runs the Basse Corniche between Nice and Menton for a couple of euros; the Moyenne Corniche line serves Èze village, and Monaco's CAM buses cover the Principality and La Turbie.

From roughly 1 July to 30 September the Alpes-Maritimes prefecture publishes a daily fire-risk map, and access to the wooded massifs, including the Grande Corniche park, can be closed outright. Check the prefecture site the night before.
Monaco's public lifts and escalators are free and run from early morning to around midnight, the fastest link between port, station and Jardin Exotique.
Heat, not gradient, is the hazard. From May the south-facing limestone reflects hard and there is no shade above 400 m; start before 07:00.
The Grand Prix, usually the last weekend in May, closes streets and triples room rates. Plan around it.

proTips: Run every climb in the morning and every coastal path in the afternoon. The ridges face south and east; by 11:00 in spring they are ovens, while the Sentier du Littoral stays half-shaded.
Use the train as a chairlift. Descending 800 m to a station and riding one stop home is far kinder on quads than reversing your climb, and a single ticket costs less than a coffee.
The Col de la Madone is a road pass, so it always has a legal, gradient-consistent escape route. Make it your turning point when weather or legs go wrong on Day 5.
Fill up at La Turbie every time you pass, its fountain sits on four of the week's seven routes.
Buy running food at the Condamine market, not at a Monte-Carlo café, the price differential is roughly fourfold.

packingNotes: Shoes with firm lugs for dry, dusty limestone. Grip here is a dust-on-rock problem, not a mud problem.
Two-litre carrying capacity for Day 5 and a 500 ml flask for everything else.
Electrolyte tablets, sweat rates on a south-facing Riviera ridge run high.
A cap, sunglasses and high-factor sunscreen, 90 per cent of this week is shadeless.
Lightweight windproof for the ridge above the Madone, where the mistral's tail end can cut ten degrees off the temperature.
Swim shorts: Larvotto and Plage Mala are legitimate recovery tools.
Offline maps: the GR51 and the local yellow waymarks overlap confusingly around the Grande Corniche.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Fire closure in summer.** If the massifs shut, everything above 300 m is off. Fall back on the coastal paths, Cap d'Ail, Cap Martin and the Menton stairways give 15 km and 500 m without entering the woods.

**Heat exhaustion on Day 5.** Thirty kilometres with 1,750 m of ascent in Riviera sun is a genuine risk. Break it at Sainte-Agnès, descend to Menton and take the train, you lose the traverse, not the week.
**Expecting Mont Agel's summit.** It is a closed military installation and the fences are real. Plan the ridge and the golf-course shoulder instead, and do not push past signage.
**Grand Prix or a race weekend.** Roads close, trains fill and prices spike. Check the Monaco events calendar before booking flights.
**Assuming Monaco is the running.** It is the bed, the food and the station. The routes are French, and every day from Day 2 crosses an unmarked border repeatedly.
